newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh death sentence draws muted relief.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh death sentence draws muted relief.

text.p: Timothy McVeigh's death sentence drew a relieved, but muted reaction across the United States on Friday, perhaps reflecting polls showing many Americans had long ago condemned him in their own minds.

"The punishment fits the crime," said a grim James Denny, whose children were severely injured in the blast. He was among a subdued crowd who awaited the decision outside the site of the federal building in Okalahoma City where 168 died in the blast McVeigh was convicted of setting off.

"The sense of relief for me personally came after the guilty verdict," he told CNN. "We knew then we had one more terrorist off the street. There will never be closure. There will always be a deep, deep hurt."
"I'm not shocked," said Anne Miller, 37, who was pushing her infant son Vincent in a stroller down a Kansas City, Missouri, sidewalk when the verdict was announced.

"With such a heinous crime, if you wouldn't give the death penalty then when would you?" she said. "If there was ever an exception, this is a time an exception should be made for those who don't believe in the death penalty," she added.

Diane Clements, president of a victims' rights group, Justice for All, said in Houston: "He is the worst human rights violators that this country has ever seen. He brought terrorism to our soil as a native son...He deserves to die. It's an American tragedy all the way around."
Brian Coyne, a 23-year-old messenger from Norwood, Massachusetts, said: "I think death would be the best thing because if you don't give it to him, how could you possibly execute anyone else?"
"On the other hand, I'd rather see him suffer in prison," he added.

Dave Bishop, 35, an engineer in Boston, said: "McVeigh believes he is, and he wants to be, a martyr. And they're giving him what he wants...He wants to be a symbol for the cause. He fought against the government and they crushed him."
There was little of the applause, shouting or cheering that greeted McVeigh's earlier conviction.
Paul Heath, speaking for the Oklahoma City Survivors Association, said before the verdict that polls indicated the U.S. populace backed execution for McVeigh by a 70-30 margin.

Among those who opposed it, and capital punishment in general, were the U.S. Roman Catholic bishops. Some newspapers had called for death in advance, but others, like the Madison, Wisconsin, Capital Times, wanted McVeigh spared, saying in a recent editorial: "We do not need another death."
Raja Arabolu, 40, an insurance salesman in West Hartford, Connecticut, said: "I don't believe in the death penalty, but I'm torn in this one, because he caused a tremendous amount of harm."
"Emotionally, yes, I believe he should pay for the crime. But the bottom line is that I believe that we, as the human race, do not have the right to take somebody else's life," he said.

"I'm glad its over," Roy Sells, whose wife died in the explosion, told CNN. "I got what I wanted. I thought he should have death and that's what he got. It's not a lot of fun to put a guy to death, but it wasn't a lot of fun when he put our loved ones to death either."
Acclaimed defence attorney Alan Dershowitz said McVeigh's lawyers had presented "an awful, awful defence" that "gave the jury very little to work with."

The Harvard law professor, interviewed by telephone on CNN, said he expected the leading defence lawyer Stephen Jones to be fired, even before an appeal that Jones has said he would file on McVeigh's behalf.
